sectionIntros.cwv: Core Web Vitals are Google's key metrics for measuring real-world user experience. They focus on loading performance (LCP), interactivity (FID/INP), and visual stability (CLS). Scores are compared against Google's thresholds for Good, Needs Improvement, and Poor performance. Meeting the Good thresholds for all three metrics is essential for optimal search rankings.
sectionIntros.lighthouse: Lighthouse provides automated auditing across Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, and SEO categories. Each category score reflects adherence to web development best practices. This section shows the scores for each Lighthouse audit category as measured during the analysis.
sectionIntros.resources: Resource analysis examines the composition of your page — scripts, stylesheets, images, fonts, and other assets. Understanding your resource breakdown helps identify optimization opportunities. Reducing the number and size of resources directly improves load times and Core Web Vitals scores.
sectionIntros.network: Network performance metrics measure how quickly your server responds and delivers content. Time to First Byte (TTFB) indicates server processing speed, while DNS lookup and SSL negotiation times reveal connection overhead. Optimizing these metrics requires attention to both server configuration and network infrastructure.
sectionIntros.caching: Effective caching reduces server load and dramatically improves repeat-visit performance. Properly configured cache headers ensure browsers store and reuse static resources. This section evaluates your caching strategy, identifying resources that could benefit from longer cache durations.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the performance analysis, these recommendations target the most impactful improvements. Addressing high-priority items first will deliver the greatest gains in load time and Core Web Vitals scores.
sectionIntros.dimensionalGrades: This section provides a multi-dimensional view of your site\
sectionIntros.crossBrowser: This section compares performance between desktop and mobile environments. Mobile users often experience slower performance due to network conditions and device constraints. Understanding the gap between desktop and mobile helps prioritize optimization efforts for the platform most of your visitors use.

accessibility.title: Accessibility Analyzer
accessibility.subtitle: WCAG Compliance & A11y Audit
accessibility.pageIntro: This report tests your website against WCAG 2.1 guidelines, checking color contrast, keyboard navigation, ARIA labels, and screen reader compatibility. An inaccessible site excludes users with disabilities and exposes you to legal risk. Use these results to make your site usable for everyone.

sectionIntros.wcag: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 define standards for making web content accessible to people with disabilities. Compliance is measured across four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust. This section evaluates your page against key WCAG Level AA success criteria. Meeting these standards ensures your site is usable by the widest possible audience and may be required by law in many jurisdictions.
sectionIntros.contrast: Sufficient color contrast ensures that text and interactive elements are readable by people with low vision or color vision deficiencies. WCAG 2.1 Level AA requires a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. This section identifies elements that fail to meet these thresholds. Fixing contrast issues is one of the most impactful accessibility improvements you can make.
sectionIntros.keyboard: Keyboard accessibility ensures that all interactive elements can be reached and operated using only a keyboard. This is essential for users who cannot use a mouse due to motor disabilities, as well as power users who prefer keyboard navigation. This section checks for focusable elements, tab traps, and visible focus indicators. Every interactive element must be reachable via Tab key and operable via Enter or Space.
sectionIntros.aria: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes and semantic HTML provide the foundation for screen reader accessibility. Proper use of landmarks, labels, roles, and heading structure allows assistive technology to navigate and understand your page. This section checks for ARIA implementation quality, landmark regions, form labels, and heading hierarchy. Incorrect ARIA usage can actually make accessibility worse, so proper implementation is critical.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the accessibility audit, this section provides prioritized recommendations to improve your site's inclusivity. Each recommendation references the relevant WCAG success criterion and includes practical steps for implementation. Addressing high-priority items first will yield the greatest improvement in accessibility compliance and user experience for people with disabilities.

security.title: Security Analyzer
security.subtitle: SSL, Headers & Vulnerability Scan
security.pageIntro: This report scans your website for SSL configuration, security headers, cookie policies, and known vulnerabilities. Security gaps put your visitors at risk and erode trust in your brand. Follow the recommendations to harden your defenses and meet modern security standards.
security.helperText: Tests SSL/TLS, security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options), and OWASP-aligned checks.

sectionIntros.ssl: SSL/TLS certificates establish encrypted connections between your server and visitors, protecting data in transit. A valid, properly configured certificate is essential for user trust and search engine rankings. This section evaluates your certificate validity, protocol version, issuer, and expiration status. Modern sites should use TLS 1.2 or higher and ensure certificates are renewed well before expiration.
sectionIntros.headers: Security headers instruct browsers on how to handle your site's content, providing defense against cross-site scripting, clickjacking, and other common attacks. Each header serves a specific protective function. This section evaluates the implementation of critical security headers and identifies missing protections that leave your site vulnerable.
sectionIntros.vulnerabilities: This section identifies potential security vulnerabilities discovered during the analysis. Vulnerabilities are categorized by severity level — critical issues require immediate attention, while lower-severity findings represent opportunities to strengthen your security posture. Regular vulnerability assessments are essential for maintaining a secure web presence.
sectionIntros.cookies: Cookies store session data and user preferences, making their security critical for protecting user privacy. Properly configured cookies use the Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes to prevent theft and misuse. This section audits all cookies detected on your site and evaluates their security configuration.
sectionIntros.thirdParty: Third-party scripts extend your site's functionality but introduce security risks. Each external script is a potential attack vector if compromised. Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashes verify that fetched scripts haven't been tampered with. This section evaluates all external scripts, their loading patterns, and SRI coverage.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the security analysis, these recommendations prioritize the most impactful improvements for your site's security posture. Each recommendation includes the specific issue, its potential impact, and actionable steps for remediation.

sectionIntros.metaTags: Meta tags are the foundation of how search engines and social platforms understand your page. They control how your content appears in search results, social shares, and browser tabs. This section evaluates your title tag, meta description, Open Graph, Twitter Card, viewport, and canonical URL configurations. Properly optimized meta tags can significantly improve click-through rates and prevent duplicate content issues.
sectionIntros.headings: A well-structured heading hierarchy helps both users and search engines navigate your content. Headings create a semantic outline that communicates topic relationships and content importance. This section analyzes the distribution and proper nesting of H1 through H6 tags on your page. Best practice is to have exactly one H1 tag and use subsequent levels in logical order without skipping levels.
sectionIntros.content: Content quality directly impacts search rankings and user engagement. Search engines favor pages with substantial, well-written content that thoroughly covers a topic. This section examines word count, readability, text-to-HTML ratio, and sentence structure to assess your page's content depth. Pages with fewer than 300 words are generally considered thin content and may struggle to rank competitively.
sectionIntros.images: Images enhance user experience but can hurt SEO if not properly optimized. Missing alt text reduces accessibility for screen reader users and eliminates a key ranking signal for image search. This section checks alt text coverage, image dimensions, and file references to ensure your images are accessible and search-friendly. Properly optimized images with descriptive alt attributes can drive significant traffic through Google Image Search.
sectionIntros.links: Internal and external links form the connective tissue of the web and are a primary way search engines discover and rank pages. A healthy link profile includes a strong internal linking structure that distributes page authority and helps users navigate your site. This section evaluates the balance of internal vs. external links, nofollow usage, and any broken link patterns. Broken or malformed links can waste crawl budget and create poor user experiences.
sectionIntros.mobile: With mobile-first indexing, Google prioritizes the mobile version of your site for ranking and indexing. Over 60% of web traffic now comes from mobile devices, making responsive design essential for reaching your audience. This section tests viewport configuration, font readability, tap target sizing, and horizontal scroll issues across device sizes. Pages that fail mobile usability checks may see reduced visibility in mobile search results.
sectionIntros.structuredData: Structured data helps search engines understand your content and enables rich results such as star ratings, FAQs, and product cards in search results. Pages with rich results typically see 20-30% higher click-through rates compared to standard listings. This section checks for JSON-LD and Microdata markup, including the schema types implemented on your page. Google recommends JSON-LD as the preferred format for structured data implementation.
sectionIntros.additional: Beyond core SEO factors, several technical elements contribute to overall search health and user trust. A complete technical foundation includes proper browser identification, crawl directives, and tracking infrastructure. This section verifies the presence of a favicon, robots.txt, XML sitemap, analytics tracking, and social media links. Missing any of these elements can indicate an incomplete SEO setup and reduce your site's professional appearance.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the complete analysis, this section provides actionable code fixes and step-by-step implementation guides. Recommendations are organized by impact level so you can prioritize the changes that will deliver the greatest SEO improvements first. Each recommendation includes both the problematic pattern and the recommended solution with copy-ready code snippets. Implementing these fixes in order of severity will help you systematically improve your site's search performance.

Missing alt text is one of the most common SEO and accessibility issues.

headings.title: Fix heading structure
headings.impact: Clearer page structure improves crawlability and user engagement
headings.missingH1Detail: Your page is missing an H1 heading. The H1 is the primary heading that tells both search engines and users what the page is about. It carries the most weight of any heading tag and should contain your primary target keyword. Every page should have exactly one H1.
headings.multipleH1Detail: Your page has {{count}} H1 headings. Multiple H1 tags dilute the primary keyword signal and confuse search engines about the page topic. Keep one H1 as the main heading and demote others to H2 or H3.

links.description: External links that open in a new tab without rel="noopener noreferrer" expose your site to reverse tabnapping attacks, where the opened page can use the window.opener API to redirect your original tab to a phishing site. This is a well-documented security vulnerability that can trick users into entering credentials on a fake version of your site without realizing they have been redirected. Additionally, links with empty or missing anchor text waste valuable link equity because search engines use anchor text to understand the context and relevance of the linked page. Screen reader users also rely on anchor text to understand where a link leads before activating it, so empty anchors create a confusing and inaccessible experience. Both issues are simple to fix and should be resolved across all external and internal links.

whatIs.a: Site Mechanic is a set of website diagnostics modules (Speed & UX, SEO, Accessibility, Security, Fonts & Design, Hosting, and more). You paste a URL, run a scan, and get prioritized issues plus next-step recommendations.

accountNeeded.q: Do I need an account to run scans?
accountNeeded.a: No. Most scans can be run without signing in. If you choose a paid report/export, you may be prompted to sign in or purchase credits depending on the tool.

validUrls.a: Use a public, reachable URL (for example https://example.com). Redirects are fine. Pages behind logins or IP allow-lists may not be scannable.

scanTime.a: It depends on the module and the site. Quick scans are typically under a minute; Lighthouse audits can take a few minutes. If a site is slow or blocks automation, scans can take longer or fail.

paidReport.q: What is a "paid report" on Site Mechanic?
paidReport.a: A paid report is an export/share outcome for a specific scan, such as PDF export, share links, downloadable data, or extended fix guidance. You can usually run the scan for free and then decide whether to purchase the report.

credits.a: Credits are used to unlock paid reports for individual scans. When a report is locked, you’ll see options to buy a single report or buy a credit pack. If you already have credits, you can unlock with 1 credit.

singleReport.q: Can I buy a single report without a subscription?
singleReport.a: Yes. Many tools offer a "buy single report" option for one scan. Credit packs are also available if you run reports regularly.

refunds.a: If you’re not satisfied within the first 14 days of a subscription purchase, contact support for a refund. For one-off credit purchases, reach out and we’ll help resolve issues or correct billing mistakes.

payments.q: What payment methods do you accept?
payments.a: Payments are processed through Stripe. Most major credit/debit cards are supported. Site Mechanic does not store your full card details on our servers.

scanCount.a: A scan is when you run any analyzer (Performance, SEO, Security, etc.) on a URL. Each time you click "Analyze" or "Run Scan", it counts as one scan toward your daily limit.

reportUnlock.a: A paid report unlock gives you access to Pro features for a specific scan result: PDF export, shareable links, detailed recommendations, and saved report history. Free users can view basic scan results but need to unlock for Pro features.

planLimits.a:
Free: 10 scans per day, Pro sections are locked.
Day Pass ($20): Unlimited scans for 24 hours + 30 report unlocks.
Pro Monthly ($29/mo): Unlimited scans + 250 report unlocks per month.
Pro Annual ($290/yr): Unlimited scans + unlimited report unlocks.

dailyLimit.q: What happens when I hit my daily scan limit?
dailyLimit.a: When you reach 10 scans in a day (Free tier), the scan button is disabled until midnight UTC. You'll see upgrade options for Day Pass or Pro subscriptions to continue scanning immediately.

unlocksRunOut.q: What happens when I run out of report unlocks?
unlocksRunOut.a: For Day Pass users, you can unlock up to 30 reports during your 24-hour window. For Pro Monthly, your 250 reports reset at the start of each billing period. Pro Annual has unlimited unlocks. If you run out, you can purchase a Single Report ($5) or upgrade your plan.

dayPass.q: How does the Day Pass work?
dayPass.a: The Day Pass ($20) gives you full Pro access for 24 hours from the time of purchase. You get unlimited scans and up to 30 report unlocks during this window. It does not auto-renew—perfect for one-time projects or client presentations.

singleReport.q: How does the Single Report option work?
singleReport.a: Single Report ($5) lets you unlock one specific scan result without a subscription. After unlocking, you have permanent access to that report’s Pro features including PDF export and detailed recommendations. Great if you only need one report occasionally.

resets.a: Daily scan limits reset at midnight UTC. For Pro Monthly subscribers, report unlocks reset at the start of each billing cycle. Day Pass limits expire 24 hours after purchase.

devtoolsDiff.q: Why can results differ from what I see in Chrome DevTools?
devtoolsDiff.a: Many metrics depend on device emulation, network conditions, caching, and timing. Site Mechanic uses automated runs that may not match your exact local environment. Treat results as directional signals, then verify fixes locally.

crawlAll.q: Do you crawl my entire website?
crawlAll.a: It depends on the module. Some tools analyze a single page URL. Crawling modules (when enabled) scan multiple pages based on discovered links and limits.

localhost.q: Can you scan staging sites or localhost?
localhost.a: No. For security reasons, Site Mechanic blocks localhost and private network targets. Use a publicly reachable staging URL instead.

dataStored.q: What data is stored after I run a scan?
dataStored.a: Site Mechanic may store scan artifacts needed to generate reports (for example exported PDFs). Generated PDF files are automatically cleaned up after a retention period (7 days by default).

screenshots.a: Some reports include screenshots to make results easier to review. Screenshot/report artifacts follow the same retention approach as reports (automatic cleanup).

blockScans.a: Yes. Some sites block automated browsers, rate-limit requests, or require cookies/authentication. If a scan fails, try again, or test a different page URL.

securityFixes.title: Security Fixes
securityFixes.excellentDescription: All security checks passed. Your site follows industry best practices for SSL, headers, and vulnerability prevention.

implementHttps.summary: Your website is not using HTTPS encryption, which means all data transmitted between your server and visitors is sent in plain text. This includes passwords, personal information, payment details, and session tokens, all of which can be intercepted by attackers on the same network through man-in-the-middle attacks. Modern browsers display a prominent "Not Secure" warning in the address bar for HTTP sites, which erodes visitor trust and increases bounce rates. Google also uses HTTPS as a ranking signal, so unencrypted sites face a measurable SEO penalty. Free SSL certificates are available through Let's Encrypt, making HTTPS implementation straightforward for any website.

implementCsp.summary: Your site lacks a Content Security Policy (CSP) header, leaving it vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. CSP is an HTTP response header that tells the browser exactly which sources of content (scripts, styles, images, fonts) are allowed to load on your page. Without it, attackers who find an injection point can execute arbitrary JavaScript that steals user cookies, redirects visitors to phishing pages, or silently records keystrokes. XSS is consistently ranked among the top web security vulnerabilities by OWASP and is one of the most commonly exploited attack vectors. Implementing even a basic CSP dramatically reduces your attack surface and provides a strong defense-in-depth layer against script injection.

enableHsts.summary: HSTS header is not configured, leaving your site vulnerable to protocol downgrade attacks. When a user types your domain without the "https://" prefix, the browser initially connects over plain HTTP before being redirected to HTTPS. During that brief unencrypted request, an attacker on the same network can intercept the connection and prevent the redirect to HTTPS entirely, a technique known as SSL stripping. The HSTS header tells browsers to always use HTTPS for your domain, eliminating that initial insecure request completely. Once set, the browser remembers this preference for the specified duration and refuses to connect over HTTP, even if the user explicitly types it.

preventClickjacking.summary: X-Frame-Options header is not set, leaving your site vulnerable to clickjacking attacks. In a clickjacking attack, a malicious website loads your page inside an invisible iframe and overlays deceptive content on top, tricking users into clicking buttons on your site without realizing it. This can lead to unauthorized actions such as changing account settings, making purchases, or granting permissions to an attacker's application. The attack is particularly dangerous because the user believes they are interacting with the malicious page while they are actually performing actions on your site with their authenticated session. Adding the X-Frame-Options header or using the CSP frame-ancestors directive prevents your pages from being embedded in third-party frames entirely.

preventMimeSniffing.summary: X-Content-Type-Options header is missing, which allows browsers to override the declared content type and guess what a file actually contains. This behavior, known as MIME sniffing, means a file served as text/plain could be re-interpreted and executed as HTML or JavaScript if the browser detects script-like content inside it. Attackers exploit this by uploading files with harmless extensions (such as .txt or .jpg) that contain malicious scripts, which the browser then executes in the context of your domain. This single-line header (X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff) forces the browser to strictly respect the Content-Type you declare, blocking any attempts to execute mistyped files. It is one of the easiest security headers to implement and has no negative impact on normal site functionality.

improveCookieSecurity.summary: Cookies are not properly secured, putting user sessions and sensitive data at risk. Without the HttpOnly flag, JavaScript code running on the page—including injected malicious scripts—can read session cookies and send them to an attacker, enabling complete account takeover. Without the Secure flag, cookies are transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections where they can be intercepted on public Wi-Fi or compromised networks. The SameSite attribute prevents cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attacks by controlling whether the browser sends cookies with requests originating from other websites. Setting all three flags on your session cookies closes the most common cookie-related attack vectors with minimal implementation effort.

addSri.summary: Third-party scripts and stylesheets are loaded without integrity verification, creating a supply chain vulnerability. If the CDN or external server hosting these files is compromised, an attacker could replace the legitimate file with malicious code that executes on every page load for all of your visitors. Subresource Integrity (SRI) adds a cryptographic hash to each external resource tag, and the browser verifies the downloaded file matches that hash before executing it. If the file has been tampered with, the browser blocks it entirely, preventing the compromised code from running. This protection is especially critical for widely-used libraries like jQuery or Bootstrap, which are high-value targets for supply chain attacks.

fixSummaries.lcpOptimization: Your Largest Contentful Paint is {{value}}, which is above the {{target}} target. LCP measures how long it takes for the largest visible content element—typically a hero image, heading, or background graphic—to finish rendering on screen. This is the metric users most closely associate with perceived load speed, and Google uses it as a direct Core Web Vitals ranking factor. A slow LCP usually indicates that critical resources are not being prioritized, images are uncompressed, or render-blocking scripts are delaying the page paint. Optimizing LCP often yields the single biggest improvement in both user experience and search rankings.
fixSummaries.javascriptOptimization: Your site has {{value}} of Total Blocking Time, meaning the browser's main thread is occupied executing JavaScript and cannot respond to user input like clicks, taps, or key presses. This creates a frustrating experience where buttons appear clickable but do nothing, scroll feels janky, and forms seem unresponsive. Total Blocking Time directly measures the cumulative periods during which the main thread is blocked for more than 50 milliseconds, and it is a key component of your Core Web Vitals score. Common causes include large unminified JavaScript bundles, synchronous third-party scripts, and unused library code that is downloaded but never executed. Deferring non-critical scripts, removing unused code, and code-splitting large bundles can dramatically reduce blocking time.
fixSummaries.clsOptimization: Layout shifts are occurring during page load, causing content to move unexpectedly and disrupting the user experience. This happens when elements change position after the page initially renders—for example, an image loads without reserved dimensions, a web font swaps in with different metrics, or a dynamic ad banner pushes content down the page. These unexpected shifts are especially frustrating for users who are about to tap a button or read text that suddenly jumps to a different location, often causing accidental clicks. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is one of Google's three Core Web Vitals metrics and directly affects your search rankings. The most effective fixes include adding explicit width and height attributes to images, using font-display: swap with size-adjusted fallback fonts, and reserving space for dynamic content.
fixSummaries.imageOptimization: Images typically account for the largest portion of total page weight, often consuming 50-80% of all downloaded bytes. Unoptimized images—those served in older formats like JPEG or PNG, at unnecessarily high resolutions, or without responsive sizing—force visitors to download megabytes of data they may not need. This dramatically increases load time, especially on mobile networks where bandwidth is limited and data may be metered. Modern image formats like WebP and AVIF can reduce file sizes by 60-80% compared to JPEG with no visible quality loss. Combining format optimization with responsive srcset attributes and lazy loading for below-the-fold images typically produces the single largest performance improvement for most websites.
fixSummaries.accessibilityImprovements: Your site's accessibility score indicates that users with disabilities may encounter significant barriers when trying to use your website. Common issues include images without descriptive alt text (which prevents screen reader users from understanding visual content), insufficient color contrast (which makes text unreadable for users with low vision), and form inputs without associated labels (which makes forms unusable with assistive technology). Accessibility is not only an ethical obligation but increasingly a legal requirement under the ADA, Section 508, and the European Accessibility Act, with non-compliance leading to lawsuits and fines. Search engines also factor accessibility into rankings, as many accessibility best practices align with SEO fundamentals like semantic HTML and clear content structure. Addressing these issues improves the experience for all users, not just those using assistive technology.

sectionIntros.overview: Mobile optimization is critical as over 60% of web traffic comes from mobile devices and Google uses mobile-first indexing. This overview presents your aggregate mobile score and key performance indicators across tested device configurations. A strong mobile experience directly impacts search rankings, user engagement, and conversion rates.
sectionIntros.touch: Touch target sizing ensures interactive elements are easily tappable on touchscreen devices. Google recommends touch targets be at least 48x48 CSS pixels with adequate spacing. This section identifies elements that are too small or too close together, which can frustrate mobile users and increase error rates.
sectionIntros.readability: Mobile readability encompasses font sizing, line height, contrast, and text layout on small screens. Text that is too small, has poor contrast, or requires horizontal scrolling creates a poor reading experience. This section evaluates your content's readability across mobile viewport sizes.
sectionIntros.responsiveness: Responsive design ensures your layout adapts properly across different screen sizes and orientations. This section evaluates viewport configuration, media query usage, and layout behavior to identify issues that may cause content to overflow or display incorrectly on mobile devices.
sectionIntros.viewport: Viewport meta configuration and Progressive Web App (PWA) readiness determine how your site behaves on mobile devices. A properly configured viewport prevents unwanted zooming and scaling. PWA features like a web manifest and service worker enable app-like experiences.
sectionIntros.accessibility: Mobile accessibility focuses on ensuring your site is usable by people with disabilities on mobile devices. This includes touch target accessibility, screen reader compatibility, and gesture-based navigation support. Key considerations:

dataSubjectRights.step1: Create a "Your Rights" page - Add a dedicated page explaining all GDPR rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, restriction, objection)
dataSubjectRights.step2: Add request forms - Create online forms for each right type with clear submission process
dataSubjectRights.step3: Set up handling process - Define internal workflow for responding to requests within 30 days
dataSubjectRights.step4: Train your team - Ensure staff know how to verify identity and process different request types
dataSubjectRights.step5: Link prominently - Add links to rights page in footer, privacy policy, and account settings
dataSubjectRights.step6: Document everything - Keep records of all requests received and how they were handled

privacyContact.step1: Designate a DPO - Appoint a Data Protection Officer if required (public authority, large-scale processing, special categories)
privacyContact.step2: Create contact page - Add dedicated privacy contact section with email, phone, and postal address
privacyContact.step3: Set up privacy email - Create a dedicated privacy@yourcompany.com inbox monitored daily
privacyContact.step4: Define response SLA - Commit to responding to privacy inquiries within 48 hours
privacyContact.step5: Add to privacy policy - Include full contact details in your privacy policy header
privacyContact.step6: Provide escalation path - List supervisory authority contact for users who want to lodge complaints

consentWithdrawal.step1: Add cookie settings link - Provide a persistent "Cookie Settings" link in footer to re-open consent dialog
consentWithdrawal.step2: Email unsubscribe - Include one-click unsubscribe in all marketing emails (not just a preferences link)
consentWithdrawal.step3: Account settings - Add privacy preferences section in user account with toggle switches
consentWithdrawal.step4: Make it equally easy - GDPR requires withdrawal to be as easy as giving consent - no dark patterns
consentWithdrawal.step5: Process immediately - Withdrawal should take effect instantly, not "within 24 hours"
consentWithdrawal.step6: Keep consent records - Log when consent was given AND when it was withdrawn for compliance

dataRetention.step1: Audit your data - List all types of personal data you collect and where it's stored
dataRetention.step2: Define retention periods - Set specific timeframes for each data type based on legal/business need
dataRetention.step3: Document justification - Record why you need to keep data for the stated period
dataRetention.step4: Implement auto-deletion - Set up automated processes to delete data when retention expires
dataRetention.step5: Publish retention schedule - Add a clear table in your privacy policy showing all retention periods
dataRetention.step6: Review annually - Schedule yearly review of retention periods to ensure they're still justified

ageVerification.step1: Determine your age threshold - GDPR default is 16, but varies by country (UK: 13, Germany: 16, etc.)
ageVerification.step2: Add age gate - Implement age verification before account creation or data collection
ageVerification.step3: Parental consent flow - Create process for users under threshold to get parent/guardian approval
ageVerification.step4: Verify parental consent - Implement reasonable method to verify guardian identity
ageVerification.step5: Child-friendly language - If children can use your service, ensure privacy info is age-appropriate
ageVerification.step6: Special data protection - Minimize data collection from minors and never use for marketing

cookieConsent.step1: Choose a CMP - Select a GDPR-compliant Consent Management Platform (Cookiebot, OneTrust, etc.)
cookieConsent.step2: Scan your cookies - Audit all cookies set by your site and categorize them (essential, analytics, marketing)
cookieConsent.step3: Equal prominence - Show Accept and Reject buttons with equal visual weight - no dark patterns
cookieConsent.step4: Block until consent - Ensure non-essential cookies are blocked until explicit consent is given
cookieConsent.step5: Granular control - Allow users to accept/reject by category, not just all-or-nothing
cookieConsent.step6: Test thoroughly - Use browser DevTools to verify no cookies are set before consent

privacyPolicy.step1: Use a template - Start with a GDPR-compliant template and customize for your business
privacyPolicy.step2: Required disclosures - Include: data controller, DPO contact, data types, legal basis, retention, rights, transfers
privacyPolicy.step3: Plain language - Write in clear, understandable terms - avoid legal jargon where possible
privacyPolicy.step4: Layered approach - Provide a summary at top with links to detailed sections below
privacyPolicy.step5: Version control - Date your policy and keep archives of previous versions
privacyPolicy.step6: Prominent placement - Link in footer, signup forms, checkout, and consent banner

tracker.step1: Audit all scripts - Use a tool like Ghostery or browser DevTools to identify all third-party trackers
tracker.step2: Document each tracker - List what data each tracker collects and for what purpose
tracker.step3: Remove unnecessary - Delete any trackers you don't actively use or need
tracker.step4: Implement consent - Ensure trackers only fire after user consent is given
tracker.step5: Update privacy policy - List all third-party processors in your privacy policy
tracker.step6: Data Processing Agreements - Ensure you have DPAs with all third-party tracker providers

sectionIntros.consent: Cookie consent mechanisms are required under GDPR and ePrivacy regulations. A compliant consent banner must be clearly visible, offer granular choices, and not pre-select non-essential cookies. This section evaluates whether a consent management platform is detected and if it meets regulatory requirements.
sectionIntros.privacy: A comprehensive privacy policy is a legal requirement under GDPR. It must clearly explain what data you collect, how you use it, who you share it with, and how users can exercise their rights. This section checks for the presence and completeness of your privacy policy.
sectionIntros.cookiePolicy: A dedicated cookie policy provides detailed information about the cookies your site uses. It should explain each cookie's purpose, duration, and whether it's essential or optional. This section evaluates your cookie policy's presence and completeness.
sectionIntros.rights: GDPR grants individuals specific rights over their personal data, including access, rectification, erasure, and portability. Your site must provide clear mechanisms for users to exercise these rights. This section checks for the availability of data subject rights mechanisms.
sectionIntros.cookies: This cookie audit catalogs all cookies and tracking technologies found on your site. Each cookie is classified by purpose, security attributes, and regulatory category. Understanding your cookie landscape is essential for maintaining accurate consent mechanisms and privacy compliance.
sectionIntros.risks: Risk assessment identifies potential compliance gaps and their severity. High-risk issues may expose your organization to regulatory enforcement action. This section prioritizes risks based on their potential impact and likelihood of regulatory scrutiny.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the GDPR compliance analysis, these recommendations prioritize the most critical compliance gaps to reduce regulatory risk and improve user privacy.
sectionIntros.consentQuality: This section evaluates the quality of your cookie consent implementation against GDPR requirements. Each factor is scored individually, covering banner presence, reject options, granular controls, consent library, and pre-consent cookie blocking.
sectionIntros.legalPages: This section checks for the presence of essential legal pages required for GDPR compliance: a privacy policy, a cookie policy, and terms of service. Missing legal pages represent significant compliance gaps.
sectionIntros.cookieClassification: Cookies are classified by purpose to help you understand which require consent under GDPR. Only strictly necessary cookies are exempt from consent requirements. All other categories (functional, analytics, marketing, social) require explicit user consent before being set.
sectionIntros.trackerAnalysis: Third-party trackers collect user data and require explicit consent under GDPR. This section classifies detected trackers by category and evaluates their impact on user privacy. Reducing unnecessary trackers improves both compliance and page performance.

sectionIntros.overview: The crawl overview summarizes the scope and results of the site crawl. It shows how many pages were discovered, the maximum depth reached, and overall crawl performance. Understanding your site's crawlable structure helps ensure search engines can efficiently index all your important content.
sectionIntros.pages: This section lists all pages discovered during the crawl with their HTTP status codes, titles, and response times. Pages with errors or slow response times may be hurting your search engine visibility and user experience.
sectionIntros.structure: Site structure analysis examines how your pages are organized and interconnected. A well-structured site has a shallow, logical hierarchy that enables both users and search engines to find content efficiently. Deep or orphaned pages may receive less crawl budget and link equity.
sectionIntros.issues: Issues detected during the crawl include broken pages, missing titles, duplicate content, and other technical SEO problems. Each issue is categorized by severity to help you prioritize fixes that will have the greatest impact on search performance.
sectionIntros.performance: Page performance across your site reveals patterns in response times and server behavior. Consistently slow pages may indicate server capacity issues or inefficient code. This section highlights the slowest pages and overall response time distribution.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the site crawl analysis, these recommendations target the most critical structural and technical issues affecting your site's search engine crawlability.

sectionIntros.overview: This section provides an overview of all marketing, analytics, and tracking tags detected on your page. A healthy tag implementation uses a tag management system, avoids duplicates, and loads scripts efficiently. Too many tags can slow page performance and create data quality issues. This analysis identifies each tag, its category, and how many instances were found.
sectionIntros.issues: This section highlights implementation issues and conflicts found among your tags. Common problems include duplicate tracking pixels, migration gaps between analytics versions, missing consent management, and conflicting scripts. Each issue includes severity level and a specific recommendation for resolution. Addressing these issues improves data accuracy and site performance.
sectionIntros.categories: Tags are organized by functional category to provide a clear picture of your marketing and analytics stack. This breakdown helps identify redundancies, gaps in coverage, and opportunities for consolidation. A well-organized tag infrastructure typically uses one tool per function with clear data ownership. Review each category to ensure every tag serves a specific, non-overlapping purpose.
sectionIntros.performance: Marketing tags and tracking scripts can significantly impact page load performance. Synchronous scripts block rendering while they load, and inline scripts add to the initial HTML payload. This section analyzes script loading methods, identifying blocking scripts that should be converted to async or defer loading. Optimizing script loading can reduce Time to Interactive by hundreds of milliseconds.
sectionIntros.thirdParty: Third-party scripts are loaded from external domains and include analytics libraries, advertising pixels, and CDN-hosted utilities. Each external script introduces a dependency on another server's availability and performance. This section catalogs all third-party scripts by host, category, and loading method. Minimizing third-party dependencies and ensuring proper async loading reduces performance risk.
sectionIntros.dataLayer: The dataLayer is a JavaScript array used by Google Tag Manager to pass structured data between your website and marketing tags. A well-implemented dataLayer centralizes event tracking and enables consistent measurement across all tags. This section checks for dataLayer presence, event count, and ecommerce implementation. A robust dataLayer is the foundation of accurate marketing analytics.
sectionIntros.cookies: Cookies set by tags and third-party scripts carry privacy and compliance implications. Under GDPR, CCPA, and similar regulations, users must be informed about cookies and in many cases give consent before non-essential cookies are set. This section audits all detected cookies, their vendors, purposes, and security attributes. Understanding your cookie landscape is essential for privacy compliance.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the tag intelligence analysis, this section provides prioritized recommendations to optimize your tag implementation. Recommendations cover performance optimization, data quality improvement, privacy compliance, and infrastructure consolidation. Implementing these changes will result in faster page loads, more accurate tracking data, and better compliance with privacy regulations.
sectionIntros.waterfall: The tag load waterfall shows the timing and sequence of script loading on your page. Scripts that load early and block rendering have the greatest performance impact. This visualization helps identify opportunities to defer or async-load scripts to improve page load times.

performance.loadTimeQuickWinDesc: At {{seconds}}s load time, reducing Time to First Byte through server-side caching or CDN deployment provides the fastest path to improvement. Target under 2.5s for good user experience.
performance.deliveryConnection: Load time, page size, and request count form the delivery chain — optimizing all three together yields compounding improvements
performance.pageSizeReason: Total page size is {{size}}MB. Heavy pages are especially painful on mobile networks where bandwidth is limited.

sectionIntros.families: Font families define the typographic identity of your site. This section catalogs all font families detected on your page, including their weight variants, styles, and loading sources. Using too many families increases page weight and load times. Best practice is to limit your site to 2-3 font families with only the weight variants you actually use.
sectionIntros.providers: Font providers determine how fonts are delivered to your visitors. Third-party providers like Google Fonts and Adobe Fonts offer convenience but introduce external dependencies and potential privacy concerns. Self-hosting fonts gives you full control over delivery and eliminates third-party requests. This section identifies all font sources and their delivery methods.
sectionIntros.loading: Font loading speed directly impacts First Contentful Paint (FCP) and overall perceived performance. Slow-loading fonts cause invisible text (FOIT) or flash of unstyled text (FOUT), degrading user experience. This section evaluates loading time, estimated bandwidth cost, and the impact on rendering performance. Using font-display: swap and preloading critical fonts are key optimization strategies.
sectionIntros.privacy: Loading fonts from third-party CDNs sends visitor IP addresses and browsing data to external servers. Under GDPR and similar privacy regulations, this may require explicit user consent. Google Fonts has been the subject of GDPR enforcement actions in several EU countries. This section identifies privacy implications of your font loading strategy and highlights potential compliance risks.
sectionIntros.delivery: Font delivery optimization ensures fonts are downloaded efficiently. Using modern formats like WOFF2 reduces file sizes by 30-50% compared to older formats. This section analyzes font file requests, formats, sizes, and loading times. Implementing preconnect hints for external font servers and preloading critical font files accelerates delivery.
sectionIntros.stability: Layout stability during font loading prevents jarring visual shifts that frustrate users and hurt Core Web Vitals scores. Proper fallback font stacks and font-display settings minimize Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). This section analyzes your fallback stacks, font-display usage, and CLS risk factors. Using size-adjusted fallback fonts with metric overrides can virtually eliminate font-related layout shift.
sectionIntros.advanced: Advanced typography features like variable fonts, subsetting, and unicode-range can significantly reduce file sizes and improve performance. Variable fonts combine multiple weights and styles into a single file, reducing HTTP requests. Subsetting removes unused glyphs, and unicode-range allows the browser to download only needed character sets. This section checks for adoption of these modern optimization techniques.
sectionIntros.performance: This section shows how typography impacts page performance. Metrics include page load timing, font family and variant counts, and typography scale consistency. Fewer families and weights mean faster loading. A consistent type scale improves readability and design quality.
sectionIntros.recommendations: Based on the font analysis, this section provides actionable recommendations to optimize your typography stack. Each recommendation targets a specific area — from reducing file sizes with modern formats to improving layout stability with proper fallback chains. Implementing these changes can improve both performance metrics and user experience across all devices.
